newsitem.title: POLAND: Fundementals, NBP to save zloty from crown fate.
newsitem.headline: Fundementals, NBP to save zloty from crown fate.

text.p: The Polish zloty's nearly 2.5 percent slide against the currency basket, a ripple effect of the Czech crown's drop, may be reversed by Polish fundamentals and some help from the central bank, analysts said.

They said the zloty, trading at an all-time low against its basket on Tuesday, was not headed for a crown-style plunge as the economy was sound and capital inflows here were focused on direct, not portfolio investment.

"The situation with the crown will not be repeated here as the zloty is more tightly controlled by the central bank, inflows are mainly strategic, not portfolio and fundamentals are better," said Krzysztof Bledowski, chief economist at WoodCommerz in Warsaw.
On Tuesday the zloty closed at about 0.36 percent above the parity rate after falling to the parity rate during the day, down from levels around 2.5 percent above parity last week.

Analysts said the downward pressure on the zloty should disappear in the medium-term in the face of the fast growing economy which, in contrast to the Czech Republic's, has already been largely restructured.
Strong fundamentals and relatively high interest rates had created a strong appreciation pressure on the currency just days before the Czech crown problems began.

"Poland's capital markets are better regulated than the Czech Republic's, imports are more investment oriented and Poland has already restructured its economy...so the fall of the zloty is purely speculative," said James Oats, economist at UBS in London.
However, analysts said the zloty might weaken further in the short-term, as the more nervous investors sell-short Central European securities in order to cut losses.
"In the medium-term the outlook is positive for the zloty after a modest weakness in the short-term...with the NBP prepared to act if necessary," UBS's Oats said.
Analysts said the NBP may have to use some of Poland's nearly $18 billion currency reserves to keep the zloty from falling sharply during periods of heavy investor withdrawal.

Many Polish forex market dealers expected the central bank to begin selling currencies if the zloty fell below the parity rate, which serves as the mid-point for the local unit's 14-percent daily trading band.
"A large part of the market expects the NBP to intervene if the zloty falls below parity," said Witold Wozniak, forex dealer at Deutsche Bank Polska SA.

Analysts said capital inflows surrounding the upcoming flotation of Poland's largest commercial bank, Bank Handlowy SA, and copper giant KGHM Polska Miedz SA, would help create upward pressure on the zloty.
"Handlowy and KGHM (IPOs) will create large inflows and could serve as a warning for currency speculators," one London-based analyst said.

Analysts said that in the end what may have saved the zloty from a large scale devaluation was the general view that Poland was not yet accessible to the average international investor, a tag which the Czech Republic had managed to shed.

"The same kind of attack on the currency as we have seen in the Czech Republic is very unlikely as Poland doesn't have the same general investor perception of the country," said Roger Monson, chief equity strategist at Daiwa in London.
